challenges.name: Bond Streak
challenges.note: Nine correct actions in a row

hazards.engine-running-fuel-hazard: That starts the APU while the fuel transfer is live. An APU exhaust is a heat source and a potential ignition source at once, and the entire reason ground power goes on before fuelling is so nothing on the aircraft that can start a fire has any reason to run while fuel is moving nearby.
hazards.fuel-before-bond-hazard: That connects the fuel nozzle before the bonding cable is clamped to the aircraft. Fuel moving through a hose generates static charge as it flows, and without a bonded path for that charge to equalise across, the aircraft and the truck can sit at two different electrical potentials right next to a fuel vapour that only needs one spark to ignite.
hazards.smoking-ignition-hazard: That is an open ignition source inside the fuel safety zone. Fuel vapour does not stay politely at the nozzle — it drifts, and the entire reason the zone is marked and held clear is so nothing that can spark ever shares the air it drifts into.
hazards.spill-kit-missing-hazard: That starts the transfer without the spill kit staged at the connection point. A fuel connection lets go a little fuel almost every time it is broken, and the difference between a wipe-up and a reportable spill is entirely whether the kit was already there when it happened.

interrupts.alert: The bonding clamp has visibly slipped loose from the aircraft skin while fuel is still moving through the hose.
interrupts.cue: Hit the emergency fuel stop now — the bond is gone and fuel is still flowing.
interrupts.missNote: Fuel kept flowing with no bonded path between the aircraft and the truck. Every second that continued was a second the static charge building in that fuel had nowhere safe to go.
interrupts.why: A slipped clamp means the aircraft and the truck are no longer at the same electrical potential for however long the transfer keeps running, and the flow has to stop the instant that bond is lost rather than wait for someone to reach over and re-clamp it while fuel is still moving.
interrupts.wrongNote: That doesn't answer it — the lost bond is what stops this transfer, not the other way round.

interrupts.alert: A small fuel spill has started at the nozzle connection, running toward the drain grating.
interrupts.cue: Grab the spill kit now and contain it before it reaches the grating.
interrupts.missNote: The spill kept running while the deadman was held through it without anyone reaching for the kit. Fuel that reaches a drain does not stay this station's problem — it becomes the site's.
interrupts.why: A spill that reaches the drain becomes a reportable release into the site's own stormwater system, and the few seconds it takes to reach the staged kit and contain it at the source is the entire difference between a wipe-up and that outcome.
interrupts.wrongNote: Off track — the spill at the connection has to be contained before this transfer goes any further.

lateNotes.bonding-clamp: The bonding cable is clamped to the aircraft before the nozzle ever touches it, not connected afterward once fuel is already about to move.
lateNotes.fuel-nozzle: The bonding cable comes off last, after the nozzle is already disconnected, not before.

name: Ground Power & Static Bonding Before Fuel

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Hi-vis vest, fuel-resistant gloves and a face shield before anyone touches a hose.
steps.prompt: Hi-vis vest, fuel-resistant gloves and a face shield before anyone touches a hose.
steps.title: Suit up before fuelling
steps.why: A connection that lets go even a little fuel under pressure does it fast and close to the hands making it, and fuel-resistant gloves with a face shield are what keeps a normal splash from becoming a chemical exposure this crew has to report.

steps.cue: Confirm the fuel grade, the quantity and the ground-power sequence before staging anything.
steps.prompt: Confirm the fuel grade, the quantity and the ground-power sequence before staging anything.
steps.title: Read the fuel order
steps.why: The fuel order is what sets today's quantity and grade, and a crew that has not read it has no way to know before the truck is already connected whether the load it is about to deliver is even the one this aircraft is due.

steps.cue: Walk the ground power cart and the truck's hose. Three problems are hiding — find them by looking.

decoyNotes.sound-gpu-reel: The GPU's cable reel is wound clean and shows no damage. Nothing to flag there.

itemNames.cracked-fuel-hose: cracked fuel hose at the truck

itemNotes.cracked-fuel-hose: A cracked hose lets go fuel under pressure the moment it is charged, long before the nozzle ever reaches the aircraft.
itemNotes.damaged-plug: A damaged plug can arc on connection, and an arc is an ignition source this crew is about to work fuel next to.
itemNotes.frayed-gpu-cable: A frayed cable this close to a fuelling operation is exactly the kind of exposed conductor a fuel safety zone is built to have none of.

steps.prompt: Walk the ground power cart and the truck's hose. Three problems are hiding — find them by looking.
steps.title: Inspect the GPU and the fuel hose
steps.why: Anything with a frayed conductor or a cracked line sitting inside a zone that is about to fill with fuel vapour is a problem this crew wants to find while it is still just a maintenance item, not after it has already met the fuel it was staged next to.

steps.cue: Connect the GPU cable and confirm the engines and APU are off before fuelling starts.
steps.prompt: Connect the GPU cable and confirm the engines and APU are off before fuelling starts.
steps.title: Connect ground power
steps.why: Ground power connected first is what lets the aircraft's own engines and APU actually shut down without losing electrics on the flight deck, and nothing that can run hot or spark stays on once the fuel safety zone is about to be established around it.

steps.cue: Set the no-ignition signage around the zone and stage the spill kit at the connection point.
steps.prompt: Set the no-ignition signage around the zone and stage the spill kit at the connection point.
steps.title: Mark the fuel safety zone
steps.why: The zone only means something once it is actually marked — the signage is what tells everyone walking past exactly where the ignition-source rule starts applying, and the spill kit staged now is the kit that is actually there the moment it is needed rather than the one somebody has to go find.

steps.cue: Drive the truck in at walking pace and stop it short of the aircraft.

drag.missNote: Not stopped short — bring the truck in and stop before it reaches the aircraft.

steps.prompt: Drive the truck in at walking pace and stop it short of the aircraft.
steps.title: Bring the fuel truck in
steps.why: Every vehicle that approaches a parked aircraft on the ramp does it at walking pace and stops short of the skin — the last distance to the connection point is closed on foot with the hose, never by rolling the truck the rest of the way in.

steps.cue: Clamp the static bonding cable to the aircraft before the nozzle goes anywhere near it.
steps.prompt: Clamp the static bonding cable to the aircraft before the nozzle goes anywhere near it.
steps.title: Clamp the bonding cable
steps.why: This is the one step that has to happen before every other part of the transfer: the bonding cable is what puts the aircraft and the truck at the same electrical potential, and nothing about the nozzle, the flow or the deadman means anything for static safety until this clamp is actually on.

steps.cue: Connect the nozzle to the aircraft only now the bond is confirmed.
steps.prompt: Connect the nozzle to the aircraft only now the bond is confirmed.
steps.title: Connect the fuel nozzle
steps.why: The nozzle goes on second, never first, because everything the bonding cable was just clamped for is exactly the protection this connection needs in place before fuel starts moving through it.

steps.cue: Hold the deadman control through the fill — releasing it stops the flow instantly.
steps.holdBreakNote: Let go of the deadman mid-fill. Hold it through the whole transfer — that is what keeps fuel from moving with nobody actually watching the connection.
steps.prompt: Hold the deadman control through the fill — releasing it stops the flow instantly.
steps.title: Hold the deadman control
steps.why: The deadman control is what guarantees fuel only ever moves while someone is actually standing at the connection paying attention to it — the instant that hand comes off for any reason, the flow has to stop rather than keep running unsupervised.

steps.cue: Keep the flow rate inside the band for the whole transfer.
steps.holdBreakNote: Flow rate out of band. Bring it back to steady before the quantity overruns the order.
steps.prompt: Keep the flow rate inside the band for the whole transfer.
steps.title: Hold the transfer flow steady
steps.why: A flow that surges and drops is harder to shut off cleanly at the planned quantity, and a steady rate is what keeps the crew actually in control of the transfer instead of chasing a number that is already moving too fast to catch.

steps.cue: Read the quantity gauge and stop the transfer only once it is inside the ordered band.

gauge.label: FUEL LOAD
gauge.missNote: Outside the ordered band — confirm the quantity against the fuel order before stopping.

steps.prompt: Read the quantity gauge and stop the transfer only once it is inside the ordered band.
steps.title: Stop at the planned quantity
steps.why: The fuel order set a quantity for a reason tied to this aircraft's own weight and balance, and stopping short or running past that band hands the flight crew a load that no longer matches what the order actually planned for.

steps.cue: Disconnect the nozzle first, then the bonding cable last.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Nozzle first, then the bonding cable — the bond stays on until fuel has stopped moving entirely.
steps.prompt: Disconnect the nozzle first, then the bonding cable last.
steps.title: Disconnect in order
steps.why: The bonding cable comes off only once the nozzle is already disconnected and no fuel is moving, because reversing that order puts the aircraft and the truck back at two different potentials while there is still fuel and vapour sitting right at the connection.

steps.cue: Confirm the flight deck is ready before disconnecting ground power.
steps.prompt: Confirm the flight deck is ready before disconnecting ground power.
steps.title: Confirm before disconnecting GPU
steps.why: Ground power stays connected until the flight deck confirms they are ready to run on their own systems — pulling it early hands them an electrical transition they did not ask for at a moment they were not expecting it.

steps.cue: Log the quantity delivered, the bonding confirmation and the GPU times before signing off.
steps.prompt: Log the quantity delivered, the bonding confirmation and the GPU times before signing off.
steps.title: Log the fuel transfer
steps.why: The fuel log is what the flight crew's own weight and balance and the next shift both read — a transfer that went perfectly but never gets logged against the order leaves nothing behind to prove the aircraft actually got what it was due.
